questions.q: Which of these is the SSRF (server-side request forgery) failure mode described in the lesson?
options: A server fetching a URL generated or extracted by the model, which could point at internal infrastructure
A user forgetting their password
A model taking too long to generate a response
A model's training run crashing partway through
questions.explain: The lesson describes SSRF as a server fetching a model-generated URL that could point anywhere, including internal systems.

questions.q: What distinguishes indirect prompt injection from direct prompt injection?
options: Indirect injection only works on open-source models
Indirect injection requires physical access to the server
In indirect injection, the malicious instruction is planted in content the AI reads on the user's behalf, not typed by the user
Indirect injection is a defense technique, not an attack
questions.explain: The lesson explains indirect injection as text planted somewhere the AI reads for the user, such as a webpage, rather than typed directly into the chat.

questions.q: What is a 'backdoored' or poisoned model, as described in the lesson?
options: A model that has been fine-tuned to include a hidden trigger behavior, behaving normally except when it sees a specific phrase
A model that runs slower than average
A model that requires a password to download
A model that has been deleted from a public hub
questions.explain: The lesson describes a poisoned model as one with a hidden trigger behavior fine-tuned in, looking like a normal release otherwise.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe the 'rendered link' covert channel, at a defensive level?
options: A rendered link or auto-loading image can carry data embedded in its URL the moment it renders, without any click required
It requires the user to manually copy and paste a URL
It only works on command-line interfaces, never in chat UIs
It is purely theoretical and has no real-world relevance
questions.explain: The lesson explains that an auto-loading image or link in AI output can quietly carry data in its URL the instant it renders.

questions.q: Besides quality/pass rate, what other factors does the lesson say belong in a model comparison?
options: The model company's stock price
Cost per request/token and latency, at the volume and interactivity the application actually requires
The number of employees at the AI company
The color scheme of the provider's website
questions.explain: The lesson lists cost and latency, at real expected volume, as essential comparison axes alongside quality.

questions.q: What problem does the lesson say an eval dataset solves?
options: It reduces the AI provider's hosting costs
It turns 'I think this still works' into something you can actually demonstrate consistently, instead of relying on informal, one-off testing
It automatically writes the application's code
It eliminates the need for a system prompt
questions.explain: The lesson frames eval datasets as the fix for 'vibes-based' testing that silently breaks when something changes.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between red-teaming and Chapter 1's risk categories?
options: Red-teaming replaces the need to understand those risk categories at all
Red-teaming turns those categories from theoretical concepts into a repeatable, measured test suite run against your own application
Red-teaming only applies to risks not covered in Chapter 1
Red-teaming is unrelated to any of the Chapter 1 risk categories
questions.explain: The lesson frames red-teaming as where Chapter 1's risk categories stop being theoretical and become a repeatable, measured test suite.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why can't automated metrics fully replace human review?
options: Automated metrics are always slower than human review
Some qualities like tone and real helpfulness are genuinely subjective, and human review catches failure modes nobody thought to write a rubric for yet
Automated metrics are illegal to use in production
Human reviewers are always more accurate on every type of question
questions.explain: The lesson explains that subjective qualities and unknown failure modes are where human review still adds value beyond automated grading.

questions.q: What does knowing a provider's per-million-token pricing, as shown in this lesson, actually enable?
options: Routing simpler tasks to a cheaper model instead of defaulting every call to the most expensive option
Guaranteeing that latency will always be zero regardless of model choice
Eliminating the need to track cost once pricing is known
Making every model cost exactly the same regardless of provider
questions.explain: Since per-million-token prices can differ five to ten times across models, knowing that gap is the basis for intentionally routing cheaper tasks to cheaper models.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three things does a working alert definition actually need?
options: A favorite color, a random number, and a user's email signature
A metric to watch, a numeric threshold, and the time window that threshold is measured over
Only a metric — thresholds and time windows are optional
A screenshot of the dashboard and nothing else
questions.explain: An alert needs a specific metric, a threshold that distinguishes normal variance from a real problem, and the window that threshold applies over.

questions.q: How does this lesson say drift detection applies to an LLM app that doesn't have a classic tabular dataset?
options: Drift detection is impossible for any AI system that isn't a traditional ML model
LLM apps never experience any form of drift
Only the final production accuracy number can be tracked, nothing else
The same reference-vs-current comparison can track prompt topics, retrieved documents, or the model's own output tone and length
questions.explain: The same reference-window-vs-current-window approach extends to prompt distributions, RAG retrieval, and output characteristics in an LLM system.

questions.q: When a request's body is omitted from logging, what still remains observable, per the screenshot in this lesson?
options: Nothing at all remains visible once the body is omitted
Only the user's full name remains visible
The omitted body is still visible to anyone with the request URL
Status, model, latency, and cost keep being tracked even though the prompt and response text are dropped
questions.explain: Omitting the body doesn't mean losing all observability — operational metrics continue to flow independently of the logged text.

questions.q: According to this lesson, in which of these places can PII enter an AI system, beyond a user directly typing it?
options: Only through direct user input — no other source matters
Retrieved context in a RAG system, accumulated conversation history, and even the model's own output can all carry PII
PII can never appear in a model's output, only in its input
PII only ever appears if a developer manually inserts it into the training data
questions.explain: The lesson lists direct input, RAG-retrieved documents, multi-turn conversation history, and model output as all being places PII can show up.

questions.q: Where does this lesson say the model card format actually originates from?
options: It was invented specifically for this course and has no prior history
A 2019 research paper by Margaret Mitchell and coauthors at Google, which has since become close to a de facto industry standard
A government regulation that mandates its exact wording
It was first created by Hugging Face as a marketing tool
questions.explain: The lesson cites the 2019 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' paper as the origin, noting it has become close to a de facto standard, including on Hugging Face's hub.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the same underlying AI model could face very different compliance obligations?
options: Because compliance obligations are identical for every possible use case of a model
Because the model's obligations depend entirely on which programming language it was built with
Because risk-tiering means a model used for something like hiring (high risk) faces very different obligations than the same model used for something like game NPC dialogue (minimal risk)
Because only open-source models are ever subject to any regulation
questions.explain: Risk-tiering is based on use case, so the exact same model can land in a completely different obligation tier depending on how it's deployed.

questions.q: How does this lesson say a harmful hallucination incident should be contained, beyond just fixing the one instance?
options: By deleting all records of the incident so it cannot be referenced again
By adding the failure case to the eval dataset immediately, not just fixing that one instance
By disabling the entire AI system permanently with no further action
By ignoring it unless the exact same hallucination happens a second time
questions.explain: The lesson specifies that containing a hallucination incident means feeding it into the eval dataset so similar cases get caught going forward, not just patching the one occurrence.

questions.q: What does this lesson say 'minimum viable monitoring' for the capstone actually requires?
options: A full production-grade observability platform with real-time alerting infrastructure
Nothing at all — monitoring can be skipped for a capstone project
Logging each call's input, output, timestamp, and token count, plus one real chart of cost or latency — even a spreadsheet counts if it reflects real calls
A dedicated full-time engineering team to operate the monitoring system
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a production observability stack isn't required — logged real data plus one real chart is sufficient to prove visibility into the system's behavior.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what two things has this course built up in parallel across its first 22 lessons?
options: The discipline to evaluate an AI system before shipping it, and the discipline to watch, document, and respond to it once it's live
How to write marketing copy for an AI product and how to price it
Only how to build a chatbot, with no other skills covered
How to train a large language model from scratch
questions.explain: Chapters 1-2 focused on evaluation before shipping, and Chapters 3-4 focused on monitoring, documentation, and incident response once live — the capstone combines both.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say four separate deliverables (eval dataset, monitoring setup, incident response plan, model card) are not yet a portfolio piece on their own?
options: A portfolio piece requires a connecting narrative — a problem, how it was verified, how you'd know if it broke, and what you'd do about it — not just four separate documents
Four deliverables are already a complete portfolio piece with nothing more needed
A portfolio piece must have at least ten separate documents to be valid
Deliverables can never be turned into a portfolio piece under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the narrative connecting the four deliverables is what actually gets read and makes it a portfolio piece, not the documents in isolation.
